topic: Tardigrades surviving open space (ESA FOTON-M3 2007) and 30-year freeze revival
hook: Tardigrades survived 10 days in open space

slides.title: The 2007 space test
slides.body: In 2007, ESA flew dried tardigrades outside a capsule in orbit, exposed to space vacuum and cosmic radiation.
slides.image_prompt: Tiny translucent tardigrade floating against black space with Earth's curved blue horizon glowing below, cinematic lighting
slides.credit: Schokraie E, Warnken U, Hotz-Wagenblatt A, Grohme MA, Hengherr S, et al. (2012) (CC BY 2.5) via wikimedia

slides.title: Dried into a 'tun'
slides.body: They survive by losing almost all their body water and curling into a 'tun'. Their metabolism nearly stops.
slides.image_prompt: A shriveled, curled-up microscopic creature like a dry barrel on a moss leaf, macro view, soft green light

slides.title: Some survived raw sunlight
slides.body: Most died under full solar UV, over 1,000 times Earth's surface level. A few survived and later laid eggs.
slides.image_prompt: Intense white ultraviolet sunlight blasting across dark space onto a tiny metal capsule in orbit
slides.credit: European Space Agency (CC BY-SA 3.0 igo) via wikimedia

slides.title: Back after 30 years
slides.body: Tardigrades frozen in Antarctic moss since 1983 woke up in 2014 and went on to reproduce.
slides.image_prompt: Frosted clump of green moss inside a frozen ice block, cold blue light, tiny creature visible inside
slides.credit: NOAA Photo Library (Public domain) via wikimedia

cta: Follow for a new wild fact every day
caption:
In 2007, tiny animals called tardigrades rode on the outside of an ESA spacecraft for 10 days, exposed to vacuum and cosmic radiation. Many came home alive, and some even laid eggs.

Their trick is drying out almost completely. Others frozen in Antarctic moss for 30 years woke up and had babies. Follow @you.didnot.know for one verified fact you can't unlearn, every day.

Would you rather be able to survive space or survive 30 years frozen?
